clue.text: Medium for hiding bikini line's very unusual

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the ordinary, so these letters are set in a new order

parts.note: the S of the 's is kept, so the fodder reads bikini lines

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that their bikini line is remarkably odd, with a hint of a hidden message.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' scrambles BIKINILINES plus V (very) into the two-word answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ink that only shows when heated or treated is a medium for writing secret messages.

clue.text: With it, sauce is revolting and dry

parts.note: with it means fashionable, which is in

indicators.note: revolting here means turning over, so the words sauce and is are read upwards, last to first

parts.note: a dip is a sauce for dunking
taken as written

explanation.surface: A trendy sauce turns out disgusting and dry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With it' means trendy, and 'revolting' means turning over, not disgusting.
explanation.definitionFit: Dry in the sense of dull and lacking flavour or interest.

clue.text: Lovers find place briefly: beach on island, without publicity

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the last letter of the word for place is dropped

parts.note: a venue is a place where something happens
sand is what a beach is made of
an ad is publicity; without here means outside, setting it at the front of the run
taken as written

explanation.surface: Two lovers hunt for a spot on an island beach, keeping things quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' trims VENUE to VENU. This is Shakespeare's narrative poem about the goddess and the youth she loved.
explanation.definitionFit: The goddess and the beautiful youth she desired are a famous mythological couple, the subject of Shakespeare's poem.

clue.text: Mushy peas (I say!) dipped in sauce

indicators.note: dipped in means plunged into, so the spoken letters go inside the word for sauce

parts.note: soy is a sauce

indicators.note: I say marks what follows as speech, so peas is heard as the letters P P

parts.note: the word sounds like two letters P

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims at mushy peas dunked in sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I say' signals that peas is heard as the two letters P P; 'Mushy' is the definition, not a description of the peas.
explanation.definitionFit: Soppy and mushy are both synonyms for sentimental or soft.

clue.text: Strain chest area and wrench back

parts.note: the bust is the chest

indicators.note: back means the word for wrench is read in reverse

parts.note: to tug is to pull or wrench

explanation.surface: Someone strains their chest muscles and wrenches their back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns TUG into GUT.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for making an enormous effort, straining oneself to the limit.

clue.text: Something to sit on minutes after climbing is sack

indicators.note: after puts the minutes letter at the end
climbing in a down clue means the word for sack is read upwards

parts.note: to axe is to sack

explanation.surface: Something to sit on after climbing turns out to be a sack.
explanation.walkthrough: You sit an exam, so 'Something to sit' is the definition; 'climbing' reads upwards in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Students sit a test, so a test is something one sits.

clue.text: Wanting state banquets, perhaps, during uprising supervised

indicators.note: during means within, so the feasting word goes inside the other piece
uprising in a down clue means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to see to something is to supervise it, so supervised gives seen
banquets as a verb means feasts, one example of dines

explanation.surface: A hungry nation stages state banquets during an uprising under supervision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uprising' reads upwards in a down clue; 'banquets' is a verb, feasts, so DINES is an example of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Neediness is the condition of being in want.

clue.text: Defenders worry club will get unwanted adviser

parts.note: in football and rugby the backs are the defenders
something eating you worries you
a driver is a golf club

explanation.surface: Football defenders fret that the club will hire an unwelcome consultant.
explanation.definitionFit: A passenger who keeps telling the driver what to do is the classic unwelcome adviser.

clue.text: Sent message to Edward in Dallas perhaps, as leaving

indicators.note: leaving means the word as departs from the result
in means the name for Edward goes inside the state

parts.note: Dallas is a city in Texas, so it is an example of that state's places
Ted is a short form of Edward
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone texts Edward, who is in Dallas, as he leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts Edward inside the state before 'leaving' removes the letters of as.
explanation.definitionFit: To text someone is to send them a message by phone.

clue.text: Students returning to college give one the time of day

indicators.note: returning means the student union letters run backwards

parts.note: NUS is the National Union of Students, a UK student body
going up is going to university, so up means at or to college

explanation.surface: Students heading back to college politely greet someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns NUS into SUN. To 'give someone the time of day' is to be civil to them, but here 'time of day' is the definition. 'Going up' is British for starting at university.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunrise is a particular time of the day, the moment dawn breaks.

clue.text: Player could go by this army officer in uniform

indicators.note: in means the army officer pieces sit inside the word for uniform

parts.note: uniform as an adjective means alike, the same
the TA is the Territorial Army, the UK's volunteer reserve
GEN is the abbreviation for general

explanation.surface: An actor might be known by an army officer in uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' means an actor, not a sportsperson.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor often works under an assumed name, so a performer could be known by one.

clue.text: One seeing owl in small tree no more, in park

indicators.note: the second in says the small-tree pieces go inside the word for park

parts.note: to park something is to put it somewhere

indicators.note: no more removes the letters of the word more from the tree's name

parts.note: a sycamore is a tree

explanation.surface: Someone spots an owl perched in a small tree that no longer stands in the park.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no more' cuts MORE from SYCAMORE to leave SYCA. The definition alludes to Edward Lear's poem in which the Owl and the Pussycat go to sea.
explanation.definitionFit: In Lear's nonsense poem the cat is the owl's companion, sailing with it in a pea-green boat.

clue.text: Criticise pettily, but hardly scoff

definitions.meaning: to find small faults with, nag
scoff is British slang for eat greedily; to eat in tiny unenthusiastic bites is the opposite

explanation.walkthrough: 'scoff' here is British slang for gobbling food, not mocking.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to find fault in a niggling way and to nibble without appetite.

clue.text: Ten asses used in a run, extraordinarily

indicators.note: extraordinarily means in an unusual way, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Ten donkeys are put to work in a remarkable run.
explanation.walkthrough: The as was a Roman copper coin; the silver coin worth ten of them is the answer. 'asses' is not about donkeys.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman silver coin was originally valued at ten copper units, so it equals that sum.

clue.text: Think back of car entering playground extraordinary at first

indicators.note: entering means the car word goes inside the playground word

parts.note: a rec is a recreation ground, a British name for a public playground
of car is the possessive, Mini's, the Mini being a small British car

indicators.note: at first means only the opening letter of extraordinary is used

explanation.surface: Someone recalls a car driving into an extraordinary playground.
explanation.walkthrough: The MINI is a classic British small car; read 'of car' as MINI'S.
explanation.definitionFit: To reminisce is to recall the past fondly.

clue.text: Work that caddie, nearby wheeling bags!

indicators.note: wheeling means turning round, so the letters found are read backwards
bags means holds, so the answer lies within the words caddie nearby

explanation.surface: A golfer admires a caddie nearby wheeling a trolley of golf bags.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bags' holds DIENEA inside caddie nearby, and 'wheeling' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgil's epic poem is a literary work.

clue.text: Latin mark well short, containing a zero

indicators.note: containing means the shortened Latin phrase holds the letter a
short means the last letter is removed

parts.note: nota bene is the Latin for mark well, abbreviated NB
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Latin note that falls short, containing a nought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims NOTABENE to NOTABEN, which 'containing' wraps round A.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal idiom meaning nothing at all, as in having no money.

clue.text: Ultimately promising sign of me getting an award

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so the last letter is taken

parts.note: the Ram is the zodiac sign Aries
something of me is my

explanation.surface: A promising zodiac sign hints that I am about to win an award.
explanation.definitionFit: The music industry's annual prize is a well-known award.

clue.text: Eponymous American manages to pen article where European's failed

indicators.note: to pen means to write in, so the article goes into the phrase
where marks the spot in the phrase where the change happens
failed means the European letter is lost

parts.note: to get by is to manage
E is the abbreviation for European
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An American hero manages to write an article after a European fails.
explanation.walkthrough: A replaces the E in GETS BY. He is the title character of Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby, so 'Eponymous' is fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Fitzgerald's novel takes its title from its American protagonist, so the man is eponymous.

clue.text: My fixed training route that gives me a shapely figure!

definitions.text: that gives me a shapely figure

parts.note: my as an exclamation of surprise is cor in British slang
set means fixed
RY is the abbreviation for railway, the route a train runs on

explanation.surface: A woman praises her rigid exercise regime for giving her a good figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My!' is an exclamation, and COR is the British equivalent.
explanation.definitionFit: Corsetry is the craft of making stiffened undergarments that shape the body.

clue.text: Two years on, I go wildly fluctuating

indicators.note: wildly means out of control, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: Y is the abbreviation for year, so two years give two Ys
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: After two years, someone says they are swinging wildly up and down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wildly' mixes two Ys with ON I GO.
explanation.definitionFit: A yo-yo rises and falls on its string, so moving up and down repeatedly.

clue.text: Start to tune instruments — they are sharp

indicators.note: start to means the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: horns are brass instruments

explanation.surface: An orchestra tunes its instruments, but some notes are sharp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sharp' looks musical, but it means pointed.
explanation.definitionFit: Thorns are pointed prickles on a plant, so they are sharp.

clue.text: Lawyer and CID officer host TV programme

parts.note: a DA is a district attorney, a US prosecutor
a DS is a detective sergeant in the CID, the UK police detective branch
a host is a great crowd or army

explanation.surface: A lawyer and a detective host a television show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'host' means a multitude, not a presenter. Dad's Army is a classic BBC sitcom about the wartime Home Guard.
explanation.definitionFit: The BBC comedy about elderly Home Guard volunteers is a famous British television show.

clue.text: Blind using pole with spike

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for south, a pole
an ear is the spike of grain at the top of a cereal stalk

explanation.surface: A blind man gets about using a pole with a spike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blind' is the verb in British 'effing and blinding', cursing.
explanation.definitionFit: To blind, in the phrase effing and blinding, is to curse.

clue.text: Indian bread is too dry in odd places when rising

indicators.note: rising in a down clue means the letters are read upwards
the first, third, fifth and seventh letters are taken

explanation.surface: An Indian flatbread is too dry in places as it rises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in odd places' picks ITOR from 'is too dry', and 'when rising' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Roti is an unleavened flatbread from the Indian subcontinent.

clue.text: Fire partner, ordering mobster in

indicators.note: ordering means putting into an order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A partner in a fire, a mobster gives orders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire partner' points to the phrase fire and brimstone.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical phrase pairs fire with sulphur, the old word for sulphur being its partner.

clue.text: Closing words in French verse call for attention

parts.note: en is French for in
oi is a British shout to get someone's attention

explanation.surface: French verse ends with a cry for attention.
explanation.walkthrough: OI is British slang for 'hey!'.
explanation.definitionFit: An envoi is a short concluding stanza of a poem, the closing lines.

clue.text: Fancy anorak and blanket concealing tablets: a legal variety?

indicators.note: concealing means the other pieces hide the tablet letters inside them

parts.note: to dig something is slang for to fancy it
E is slang for an ecstasy tablet, so tablets is Es
anorak is British slang for an obsessive, a nerd
a rug is a blanket

explanation.surface: A man hides pills in a fancy anorak and a blanket, wondering if they are legal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' looks like an adjective but is a verb, to like; ecstasy pills are called Es. An anorak is British slang for a geek.
explanation.definitionFit: Such drugs are synthesised to mimic banned ones while escaping the law, a lawful kind of narcotic.
